Good morning, tech fam! Here are today's top technology updates you need to know.
What's New Today: Mitsui Chemicals is strengthening its semiconductor ambitions with an $11.6 billion deal to acquire JSR, aiming to create Japan's largest semiconductor materials producer.
Fast-Track Insights: Japanese mobility startup Newmo has raised $135 million in Series B funding, taking its total funding to $313.1 million as it targets limited driverless taxi services by 2028.
Here's a quick rundown of today's biggest tech headlines, covering major semiconductor investments, autonomous mobility, AI infrastructure expansion, India's outsourcing industry and the growing intersection of robotics and cryptocurrency.
Mitsui Chemicals to Acquire JSR in $11.6 Billion Deal
Mitsui Chemicals has agreed to acquire semiconductor materials maker JSR for $11.6 billion to strengthen its position in the global chip industry. Backed by a $ 1263.23 billion investment from Japan’s Development Bank, the deal aims to create Japan’s largest semiconductor materials producer. Mitsui targets $ 252.64 billion in additional annual profit by 2035, despite rising debt concerns.

Newmo Raises $135 Million to Expand Autonomous Taxi Services by 2028
Japanese mobility startup Newmo has raised $135 million in a Series B funding round led by KDDI, bringing its total funding to $313.1 million. Operating around 1,900 taxis across six regions, the company plans to launch limited driverless taxi services in 2028, addressing Japan’s growing driver shortage.

Can India’s Outsourcing Industry Grow with Fewer Employees?
India’s outsourcing industry is witnessing revenue growth outpacing workforce expansion as AI automates routine tasks. While companies benefit from higher productivity and lower costs, entry-level hiring is slowing, creating challenges for fresh graduates. The industry’s long-term success will depend on reskilling, talent development and creating specialized job opportunities.

Anthropic has reportedly struck a $3.4 billion deal to secure 1.7 gigawatts of gas-fired generators for its expanding AI data centers. Key Takeaways
Key Takeaways
Peter Thiel leads a $140 million Series B for offshore AI platform maker Panthalassa.
Panthalassa’s Ocean-3 uses wave energy and seawater cooling to avoid land-based data center constraints.
Commercial viability remains unproven, with northern Pacific pilots planned for 2026 and operations for 2027.
Wave-powered AI computing attracted $140 million in Series B financing this week, with Peter Thiel leading the round for Panthalassa , a Portland, Oregon company building autonomous offshore platforms that generate their own electricity, cool hardware with seawater, and transmit AI outputs by satellite.
The flagship product, Ocean-3 , stands approximately 85 meters tall and sits mostly submerged, with a buoyant upper section and a long vertical body that gives it what the company describes as a golf-ball-on-tee profile . As the platform moves with wave motion, internal hydraulics drive seawater through turbines to produce electricity consumed onboard, with no undersea power cable to shore.
AI hardware sits in protected containers below the waterline, where the surrounding ocean acts as a passive heat sink . The company says this arrangement is intended to reduce or avoid reliance on freshwater cooling systems , which represent a significant operating cost and resource constraint for conventional land-based data centers.

AI publisher Spines raises $64 million to automate book publishing — Fortune
Fedir Kryshtovskyi
09
November
2026
19:43
Spines, a platform with offices in Israel and New York that uses artificial intelligence to prepare, publish and promote books, has raised $64 million in funding. As Fortune reports , the company plans to use the funds to develop its product and expand into other English-language markets.
Funding structure
The funding package includes $29 million in a Series A-1 round led by venture firm Zeev Ventures. Aleph, NordStar, M-Fund, LionTree and angel investor Dan Senor also participated in the round. Spines will receive another $35 million as a credit facility for growth financing from investment firm Twelve.
The company did not disclose its valuation after raising the capital. According to Spines founder and CEO Yehuda Niv, its annualized revenue reached $50 million, up 400% from a year earlier.
Services for authors
Spines operates under a hybrid publishing model: authors pay an upfront fee for services, while the company also receives a share of royalties from sales. Packages cost from about $3,000 to $20,000; authors most often choose options priced at $5,000–$7,000. Authors receive 80% of net royalties, compared with 70% previously.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram .
Writers upload a completed manuscript, after which AI agents assist with editing, proofreading, layout, cover creation, preparation of e-book and print versions, translation, audiobooks and marketing campaigns. The platform distributes books through more than 100 channels, including Amazon, Barnes & Noble and Baker & Taylor.
Spines says it has published books by more than 8,000 authors, totaling about 12,000 titles. According to Niv, around 400 new writers join the service each month. The company says it publishes only books written by humans and uses software to detect AI-generated manuscripts.
According to Niv, Spines employs about 350 people, around 50 of whom work in research and development. Management and the research team are based in Herzliya, Israel, while most of the company’s employees work in Eastern Europe, the United States and Latin America.

The Oregon robot manufacturer says it stands apart because its humanoid robot, Digit, can work alongside human colleagues.

Agility Robotics entered the Nasdaq stock market on November 5, 2026, as the Oregon-based manufacturer seeks to establish a commercial market for humanoid robots . The company raised 465 million dollars through a private investment agreement the previous day to finance further engineering, manufacturing improvements, and business expansion.
Shares experienced significant fluctuations during their first trading session, falling to 8.40 dollars before recovering to close at 11.51 dollars. The company entered public markets with an estimated market capitalization of approximately 2 billion dollars, according to The Oregonian/OregonLive.

Agility operates a 70,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in Salem, where it produces Digit, a two-legged humanoid robot designed for warehouse operations. Standing just under 6 feet tall, Digit can work for up to 20 hours daily and repeatedly lift loads weighing 50 pounds.

Company co-founder Jonathan Hurst said additional engineering work remains necessary as Agility develops its technology and improves its products.
"We have a lot of engineering to continue to do and a thousand ideas of how to improve things. We just need to have that opportunity to continue doing it," said Hurst, Agility Robotics' co-founder and chief robot officer.
Agility is attempting to demonstrate that humanoid robots can become commercially viable while meeting practical workplace requirements. The company reported several customers and conditional orders with potential future value of 300 million dollars.

However, its financial performance remains a significant challenge. According to the company, sales totaled just 1.8 million dollars last year, while its losses reached 168 million dollars. The public listing is intended to demonstrate financial discipline and provide investors with greater visibility into its development progress.
Hurst described the company's ambitions as extending far beyond warehouse operations, with potential applications in factories, homes, farms, and senior care.
"What we're creating is truly the foundation of our economy. The whole definition of labor is going to be different because the thing you think of now, when you talk about labor, people won't do those things in 30 years," said Hurst.

Agility emerged from Oregon State University's robotics laboratory in 2015. It now employs 500 people, including 175 workers at its Salem factory, which opened two years ago. The company also operates a software hub in the Bay Area and a sales and engineering center in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.
Its customers include logistics company GXO and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada. Meanwhile, Agility faces competition from other technology companies developing humanoid robots, including Tesla.
